cards.front: What should you know about genetic variation?
cards.back: Variation exists between individuals of the same species due to genetic and environmental factors. Mutations create new alleles. Genetic engineering and selective breeding allow humans to modify organisms for specific purposes.

cards.front: What should you know about variation?
cards.back: Differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species. Variation can be caused by genetic factors, environmental factors, or a combination of both.

cards.front: What should you know about continuous vs discontinuous variation?
cards.back: Continuous: A range of values with no distinct categories (e.g. height, weight). Usually influenced by many genes and the environment. Shown as a line graph or histogram. Discontinuous: Distinct categories with no in-between values (e.g. blood group A/B/AB/O, eye colour). Usually controlled by a single gene. Shown as a bar chart.

cards.front: What should you know about mutation?
cards.back: A change in the DNA sequence of a gene. Mutations happen spontaneously (randomly) and continuously. Most mutations have no effect on the organism.

cards.front: What should you know about effects of mutations?
cards.back: No effect: Most mutations have no observable effect on the phenotype (the genetic code is degenerate, so some changes don't alter the protein) Harmful: Some mutations produce a protein that does not work properly, which can cause disorders (e.g. cystic fibrosis) Beneficial: Rarely, a mutation produces a new protein that gives an advantage, which can lead to evolution by natural selection

cards.front: What should you know about mutation rate can be increased by?
cards.back: ionising radiation (e.g. X-rays, UV light), and certain chemicals (e.g. chemicals in tobacco smoke). These are called mutagens.

cards.front: What should you know about genetic engineering?
cards.back: Modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic. The organism that receives the gene is called a genetically modified (GM) organism.

cards.front: What should you know about process of genetic engineering (e.g. producing human insulin in bacteria)?
cards.back: Identify and isolate the desired gene (e.g. the human insulin gene) Cut out the gene from human DNA using a restriction enzyme Cut open a bacterial plasmid (the vector) using the same restriction enzyme Insert the human gene into the plasmid using ligase enzyme (which joins DNA strands together) The plasmid is now a recombinant plasmid (contains DNA from two different organisms) Insert the recombinant plasmid into a bacterium The bacterium divides and produces human insulin, which can be harvested and purified

cards.front: What should you know about selective breeding?
cards.back: Choosing parents with the desired characteristics, breeding them together, and selecting the best offspring to breed from again. This is repeated over many generations to develop a population with the desired trait.

cards.front: What should you know about process of selective breeding?
cards.back: Choose parents with the desired characteristics from a mixed population Breed them together Select the best offspring showing the desired characteristics Breed these offspring together Repeat over many generations until all offspring show the desired characteristic

cards.front: What should you know about examples of selective breeding?
cards.back: Dairy cows — bred to produce more milk Meat cattle — bred for lean muscle/meat yield Disease-resistant crops — bred to survive fungal or bacterial infections Domestic dogs — bred for temperament, appearance, or working ability Crops for larger or tastier fruit/vegetables

cards.front: What should you know about disadvantages of selective breeding?
cards.back: Reduction in the gene pool (genetic variation decreases over generations) Inbreeding can lead to increased risk of inherited disorders (e.g. hip problems in some dog breeds) Vulnerability to new diseases (less genetic variation means less chance of resistance)
Differences in alleles inherited from parents (e.g. Eye colour, blood group, natural hair colour, inherited diseases)
Conditions an organism lives in (e.g. Accent, scars, leaf size (due to light), hair dyed a different colour, weight from diet)

cards.front: What does Both genetic and environmental mean?
cards.back: Genetics set the potential range; environment determines where within that range (e.g. Height, weight, skin colour (genetic baseline + sun exposure), intelligence)
